record.title: A SkillsBench study reports that agent-skill utility depends on model–harness fit and artifact organization
record.summary: Cheng et al. report a controlled study of agent skills on 87 SkillsBench tasks across three models and three harnesses. The same benchmark-supplied skills help some configurations and hurt others on 32 tasks (36.78%). On 23 single-skill tasks, operation-support reranking raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35–5.80 points across three selected configurations; on multi-skill tasks, stage-plan and dependency-DAG organization generally outperform simple ordering. These are author-reported preprint results based on three runs per condition. The study does not measure runtime, token or maintenance costs, and independent transfer beyond the selected task and configuration sets remains unknown.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Cheng et al. report controlled evaluations using 87 SkillsBench tasks, three models and three agent harnesses, with three executions per task and condition; reported outcomes are task-verifier pass rates.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the same benchmark-supplied skills produce both gains and losses across model–harness configurations for 32 of 87 tasks (36.78%).

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For three selected configurations, reranking five marketplace candidates by support for atomic task operations improves first-choice pass rate over relevance-first ranking by 4.35–5.80 percentage points in the study’s existing execution records.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For the same supplied skill sets, stage-plan or dependency-DAG instructions outperform simple use order in the reported overall results; DAG improves over flat organization by 6.50–11.38 percentage points across the three configurations.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The preprint does not establish that these gains transfer to other tasks, skill libraries, languages, models or harnesses, nor that they justify runtime, token and maintenance costs.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: A direct retrieval attempt of the paper-linked anonymous artifact endpoint returned HTTP 401, so no artifact files or execution records were accessed.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the reported reranking or organization gains was conducted.
The paper links an anonymous repository for data, execution records and scripts; direct retrieval of its file endpoint returned HTTP 401, so contents remain inaccessible.
The study does not establish whether pass-rate gains justify added execution, token and maintenance costs.

brief.importance_rationale: If transferable, evidence that skill utility changes across model–harness configurations and that operation support and artifact dependencies improve task success could affect agent system selection and skill authoring. The results are bounded to selected SkillsBench tasks and configurations.
limitations: This is a single-group arXiv v1 preprint; no independent reproduction was conducted.
Task pass/fail is the outcome measure; partial completion and runtime, token and maintenance costs are outside scope.
Three runs per condition leave task-level estimates sensitive to execution randomness.
The operation-support ranking uses LLM-assisted operation extraction and support labels with heuristic scores; the paper says alternative scoring or operation granularity could change rankings.
The reranking results use the existing candidate set and execution records, and were motivated by the studied task set; independent-task stability is open.
The study centers on English-language skills, 87 SkillsBench tasks and selected model–harness configurations; generalization to other skill corpora and workflows is unknown.
The paper-linked anonymous data/code endpoint returned HTTP 401 on direct retrieval; its contents were not inspected.

relationships.summary: WikiSkill studies how a persistent knowledge layer supports skill evolution across benchmarks and models; this paper studies downstream utility of existing skills across configurations, candidate selection and skill-set organization. They address complementary stages of the agent-skill lifecycle, not the same intervention or a direct replication.

The same benchmark-supplied skills help some configurations and hurt others on 32 tasks (36.78%). On 23 single-skill tasks, operation-support reranking raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35–5.80 points across three selected configurations; on multi-skill tasks, stage-plan and dependency-DAG organization generally outperform simple ordering. technical.claimed_result: Authors report cross-configuration gain/loss reversals on 32/87 tasks, 4.35–5.80 percentage-point first-choice gains after operation-support reranking, and 6.50–11.38 percentage-point DAG-over-Flat gains across three selected configurations.
technical.compute_or_cost: Runtime, token use and skill-maintenance cost are not measured; the paper identifies these as future evaluation needs.
technical.demonstrated_result: The full v1 preprint and its reported methods and tables were inspected. The measured outcomes are author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
technical.implementation_status: Research preprint with a linked anonymous artifact repository; direct retrieval redirected to its file endpoint and returned HTTP 401, so no artifact contents were inspected.
technical.mechanism: The study compares task success with and without benchmark skills across model–harness configurations, compares relevance-ranked marketplace alternatives with an operation-support reranking, and holds the supplied multi-skill set fixed while varying organization instructions among Flat, Sequence, Stage Plan and Dependency DAG.
technical.regime: 87 SkillsBench tasks across eight domains; three models crossed with three harnesses; three runs per task and condition. RQ2 uses 23 single-skill tasks and the top five retrieved marketplace candidates. RQ3 uses 41 tasks supplied with at least three skills.
technical.reproducibility: Three runs per task and condition are reported. Independent reruns and stability on held-out tasks/configurations have not been established; the linked run records and scripts were inaccessible.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within-task comparisons use the same task verifier and model–harness configuration against No-Skill; organization comparisons retain the same supplied skills/resources while varying instructions. No independent held-out replication was inspected.

brief.title: A SkillsBench study reports that agent-skill utility depends on model–harness fit and artifact organization
brief.why_it_matters: Reusable procedural instructions can help or hinder depending on what an agent can execute and how the harness coordinates multiple skills. The study offers bounded evidence that checking operational support and preserving dependencies between intermediate artifacts may matter more than topic relevance or simple ordering alone; the gains need independent, cost-aware replication.

related.summary: The SkillsBench study evaluates downstream skill utility across model–harness pairings and skill organization; GraphSkillAA evaluates a method for updating skill-graph state. They cover complementary lifecycle stages and do not independently reproduce each other.

other.title: GraphSkillAA uses addressable skill graphs and two-stage gates for targeted agent-skill updates
other.summary: The September 2026 v2 arXiv paper introduces GraphSkillAA, which represents external skills as a graph of addressable applicability, execution and exclusion fields plus typed relations. A teacher compares successful and failed executions to propose local edits; an affected-case Local Gate and a whole-update-pool Big Gate accept or roll back changes. The authors report three-seed held-out mean hard accuracies of 81.5% on SearchQA, 66.7% on LiveMath and 91.2% on DocVQA with GPT-5.6-sol, and highest reported means across nine model–benchmark comparisons in a separate SkillOpt-protocol table. These are paper-reported results, not independently reproduced evidence; the paper limits its conclusions to the tested splits, moderate graphs and primarily single-turn tasks.

other.title: WikiSkill separates raw experience, persistent knowledge, and executable skills for agent skill evolution
other.summary: Google Research and Virginia Tech introduce WikiSkill, an agent-skill evolution loop that stores immutable execution traces separately from a persistent wiki of recurring patterns/rejected proposals and from executable skills. A maintainer consolidates experience into the wiki, a proposer uses that accumulated knowledge to revise skills, and validation gating accepts or rolls back changes. Across five benchmarks and five inference models, the authors report stronger results than prior skill-evolution baselines, with a direct ablation showing a 15-point average gain from giving the skill proposer persistent wiki access while withholding it from the inference agent.
